subject: Critical Thinking
title: The Drowning Child Problem: How Much Must You Sacrifice?
description: One-minute skill: The Drowning Child Problem: How Much Must You Sacrifice?.

hook.text: You walk past a shallow pond where a child is drowning. You'd ruin your expensive clothes to save them.

buildup.text: Peter Singer's challenge: if proximity doesn't matter morally, then we're obligated to help all preventable deaths –.

discovery.text: The 'demandingness objection': if morality demands you sacrifice until you're at the level of the poorest, then.

twist.text: Some bite the bullet: Singer himself donates 40% of income. But is morality supposed to demand this much?

climax.text: The tension is real: too little sacrifice = moral failure. Too much demand = a morality nobody follows.

punchline.text: You can't save everyone. But you can save someone. The question is: do you?

quiz.question: What is the 'demandingness objection' to Singer's drowning child argument?
options: People demand too much from philosophers
If morality requires sacrificing until you're at subsistence level, it becomes impossibly demanding

details.summary: Peter Singer's drowning child thought experiment asks if you would ruin expensive shoes to save a drowning child, then argues the same logic demands donating to save distant strangers. It challenges our moral comfort with geographic distance.
details.whyItMatters: The argument forces people to confront why they ignore preventable deaths abroad while responding to local emergencies.
takeaways: Geographic distance does not reduce moral obligation
If you would save a nearby child, consistency demands helping distant ones
The argument underpins the effective altruism movement

faq.question: What is the core argument of the drowning child problem?
faq.answer: If you are morally required to save a child right in front of you at trivial cost, then you are equally required to donate to save children dying from preventable causes far away.

faq.question: What is a common objection to Singer's drowning child argument?
faq.answer: Critics argue that personal, immediate situations create stronger obligations than distant ones, and that demanding endless sacrifice would be psychologically unsustainable.
